uni-pharm-practice.title: B.Pharm · Pharmacology, Pharmacy Practice & Regulations
uni-pharm-practice.description: B.Pharm study companion for pharmacology (ANS, CVS, analgesics, CNS, antimicrobials), dispensing and counselling, and a general overview of pharmacy regulations and ethics — with dose numericals, counselling scenarios and an incident ticket lab. Regulations are general education, not legal advice. PCI subject names are topic tags only. A study companion only: it does not replace supervised clinical training or a licence.

courses.title: Pharmacology I: Autonomic & Cardiovascular Drugs
courses.summary: Receptor pharmacology, cholinergic and adrenergic drugs, antihypertensives, antianginals and anticoagulants — mechanisms, uses, adverse effects and cautions.
outcomes: Learners can explain agonists, antagonists and dose–response
Learners can predict effects of autonomic drugs
Learners can classify antihypertensives with key adverse effects
Learners can counsel on anticoagulant safety

story.title: Why some drugs block and others stimulate

scenes.text: Salbutamol opens the airways; propranolol can narrow them.
Both act on β receptors — one as agonist, one as antagonist.

steps.title: Note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training or a professional licence.

steps.title: Core ideas
steps.body: **Affinity** (binding) vs **efficacy** (response). Full agonist, partial agonist (e.g. buprenorphine at μ-opioid), antagonist (competitive — shifts curve right, surmountable; non-competitive — lowers maximum), inverse agonist. **Potency** = EC50 (lower = more potent); **efficacy** = Emax. **Therapeutic index** = TD50/ED50 — narrow TI drugs (digoxin, lithium, warfarin, phenytoin, aminoglycosides) need monitoring.

steps.title: Receptor types
steps.body: Ligand-gated ion channels (nicotinic, GABA-A), G-protein-coupled (muscarinic, adrenergic, opioid), enzyme-linked (insulin), intracellular/nuclear (steroids, thyroid hormone).

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Confusing potency with efficacy — a more potent drug is not necessarily more effective.

activity.prompt: Match the term to its meaning
pairs: Ability to produce a response once bound
Shifts dose–response curve to the right
Submaximal response even at full occupancy

quiz.q: A narrow therapeutic index drug is…

options: Can be overcome by more agonist

scenes.text: An asthmatic patient was prescribed a non-selective β-blocker for migraine and now wheezes.
Predict and prevent.

steps.title: Cholinergic
steps.body: Muscarinic agonists/anticholinesterases (neostigmine, pyridostigmine) — used in myasthenia gravis, reversal of neuromuscular block; organophosphate poisoning → excess acetylcholine (SLUDGE + bradycardia, miosis) → atropine and pralidoxime. Antimuscarinics (atropine, tiotropium, ipratropium) → dry mouth, urinary retention, tachycardia; caution in glaucoma (angle-closure) and prostatic hypertrophy.

steps.title: Adrenergic
steps.body: α1 agonists (phenylephrine) vasoconstrict; β1 ↑ heart rate/contractility; β2 agonists (salbutamol) bronchodilate. β-blockers: cardioselective (metoprolol, atenolol, bisoprolol) vs non-selective (propranolol) — non-selective ones can trigger bronchospasm in asthma and mask hypoglycaemia warning signs.

steps.title: Exam hook
steps.body: Adrenaline is first-line for anaphylaxis (intramuscular), acting on α and β receptors.

activity.prompt: Which receptor action produces this effect?

items.text: Bronchospasm in an asthmatic on propranolol
Tachycardia and pupil dilation with atropine

quiz.q: Antimuscarinics should be used with caution in…

scenes.text: A 58-year-old with hypertension develops a dry cough on his new tablet.
Identify the cause and the alternative.

steps.title: Main classes
steps.body:
- **ACE inhibitors** (enalapril, ramipril): dry cough (bradykinin), angioedema, hyperkalaemia, first-dose hypotension; contraindicated in pregnancy.
- **ARBs** (losartan, telmisartan): similar benefits, less cough; avoid in pregnancy.
- **Calcium-channel blockers** (amlodipine): ankle oedema, flushing, gingival overgrowth.
- **Thiazide/thiazide-like diuretics** (hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone, indapamide): hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, hyperuricaemia (gout), hyperglycaemia.
- **β-blockers**: not first-line for uncomplicated hypertension in many guidelines; used with compelling indications.

steps.title: Interactions
steps.body: ACE inhibitor/ARB + potassium-sparing diuretics or potassium supplements → hyperkalaemia; NSAIDs reduce antihypertensive effect and with diuretics + ACEi/ARB raise acute kidney injury risk ('triple whammy').

steps.title: Pregnancy
steps.body: In pregnancy, options such as labetalol, nifedipine or methyldopa are used under specialist care.

activity.prompt: Match the drug class to its characteristic adverse effect

quiz.q: A dry cough on enalapril can be managed by switching to…
The 'triple whammy' combination raising AKI risk is…

scenes.text: A patient on warfarin (INR target 2–3) is prescribed a new antibiotic and asks if it's okay.
Check, counsel, escalate.

steps.title: Anticoagulants
steps.body:
- **Warfarin:** vitamin K antagonist; narrow TI; INR monitoring; many interactions (e.g. some antibiotics like macrolides, fluoroquinolones, metronidazole, co-trimoxazole raise INR; enzyme inducers like rifampicin lower it); diet consistency for vitamin K foods; reversal with vitamin K ± prothrombin complex concentrate.
- **DOACs** (apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran): fewer interactions, no routine INR; renal function matters.
- **Heparins:** UFH (aPTT monitoring, protamine reversal), LMWH (enoxaparin).

steps.title: Counselling points
steps.body: Report bleeding (black stools, blood in urine, prolonged nosebleeds, severe bruising), avoid NSAIDs/aspirin unless prescribed, inform every prescriber/dentist, carry an anticoagulant card, keep INR appointments.

steps.title: Escalate
steps.body: Major bleeding or head injury on an anticoagulant → emergency care (112).

choices.label: Flag the interaction and contact the prescriber; suggest closer INR check
choices.feedback: Correct — metronidazole can markedly raise INR.

b.text: Prescriber agrees; arranges INR in 3–5 days. Counselling?

choices.label: Bleeding signs, avoid NSAIDs, keep INR test, carry card
Tell her to stop warfarin herself
choices.feedback: Never advise stopping without the prescriber.

end1.text: INR rises to 3.4; the prescriber adjusts the dose and she has no bleeding.

courses.title: Pharmacology II: Analgesics, CNS Drugs & Antimicrobials
courses.summary: NSAIDs, paracetamol and opioids, antidepressants and antiepileptics, and antimicrobial classes with stewardship — mechanisms, adverse effects and safety counselling.
outcomes: Learners can compare NSAIDs, paracetamol and opioids
Learners can recognise opioid and paracetamol overdose risks
Learners can classify antimicrobials by mechanism
Learners can apply antimicrobial stewardship

scenes.text: A customer with back pain takes ibuprofen and has a history of stomach ulcer.
What is safest?

steps.title: Note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training or a professional licence.

steps.title: Classes
steps.body:
- **Paracetamol (acetaminophen):** analgesic/antipyretic, minimal anti-inflammatory action; overdose causes liver damage (toxic metabolite NAPQI when glutathione depletes) — antidote acetylcysteine; early treatment is critical even if the patient feels well.
- **NSAIDs** (ibuprofen, diclofenac, naproxen): COX inhibition → GI ulcer/bleed, renal impairment, fluid retention, raised CV risk, asthma worsening in some. Avoid in late pregnancy.
- **Opioids** (morphine, tramadol, codeine): respiratory depression, constipation, sedation, dependence; antidote naloxone. Codeine/tramadol rely on CYP2D6 metabolism (variable response).

steps.title: Overdose
steps.body: Suspected overdose of any medicine → emergency care immediately (112), take the pack along. Do not wait for symptoms with paracetamol.

steps.title: GI protection
steps.body: If an NSAID is essential in a high-risk patient, prescribers may add a PPI; a history of ulcer is a strong reason to avoid NSAIDs.

activity.prompt: Which analgesic class does each risk belong to?

items.text: Constipation, reversed by naloxone in overdose

quiz.q: The antidote for paracetamol overdose is…
NSAIDs cause GI ulcers mainly by…
Codeine response varies because it needs activation by…

scenes.text: A student starts sertraline and feels more anxious in week one.
Expected or dangerous?

steps.title: Antidepressants
steps.body: **SSRIs** (sertraline, fluoxetine, escitalopram): onset of benefit over 2–6 weeks; early side effects — nausea, anxiety, sleep change, sexual dysfunction; hyponatraemia (elderly); bleeding risk with NSAIDs/anticoagulants; **serotonin syndrome** with other serotonergic drugs (tramadol, linezolid, St John's wort, MAOIs). Young people need monitoring for worsening mood/suicidal thoughts early on. Do not stop abruptly (discontinuation symptoms). TCAs: anticholinergic, dangerous in overdose.

steps.title: Antiepileptics
steps.body: Valproate (highly teratogenic — strict pregnancy-prevention requirements), carbamazepine (enzyme inducer; HLA-B*1502 linked SJS/TEN risk in some Asian populations), phenytoin (zero-order kinetics at higher levels, gingival overgrowth), levetiracetam, lamotrigine (rash; slow titration).

steps.title: When to get help
steps.body: Worsening mood or thoughts of self-harm → urgent help; in India call Tele-MANAS 14416 or 112 in an emergency.

statements.s: SSRIs usually take 2–6 weeks to show full benefit.
SSRIs can be stopped suddenly without problems.

quiz.q: Serotonin syndrome risk rises when SSRIs are combined with…
Gingival overgrowth is a side effect of…
Lamotrigine requires slow dose titration because of…

scenes.text: A microbiology lecture lists ten antibiotics.
Sort them by target.

steps.title: Mechanisms
steps.body:
- **Cell wall:** β-lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems), glycopeptides (vancomycin).
- **Protein synthesis:** aminoglycosides (30S; nephro/ototoxic), tetracyclines (30S; avoid in children <8 y and pregnancy — teeth staining), macrolides (50S), linezolid (50S).
- **Nucleic acid:** fluoroquinolones (DNA gyrase/topoisomerase IV; tendon rupture risk), rifampicin (RNA polymerase; orange secretions, enzyme inducer), metronidazole (anaerobes; avoid alcohol — disulfiram-like reaction).
- **Folate:** sulfonamides + trimethoprim (co-trimoxazole).

steps.title: Tetracycline and teeth
steps.body: Tetracyclines chelate calcium and stain developing teeth — a classic dental link.

steps.title: Allergy
steps.body: Penicillin allergy history: check type of reaction; anaphylaxis history → avoid β-lactams per guidance.

activity.prompt: Sort by mechanism

quiz.q: Tetracyclines are avoided in young children because of…

options: Turn body fluids orange and induce enzymes

scenes.text: A customer with a 2-day cold and sore throat asks for an antibiotic without a prescription.
Act as a steward.

steps.title: Stewardship principles
steps.body: Right drug, right dose, right duration, right route — only when needed. Most upper respiratory infections are viral and self-limiting. Antibiotics in India are prescription-only (Schedule H/H1); sale without prescription is unlawful and drives resistance. The WHO AWaRe classification (Access, Watch, Reserve) guides choices.

steps.title: Counselling
steps.body: Offer symptomatic advice (fluids, rest, paracetamol per label, salt-water gargles), safety-netting (see a doctor if high fever, difficulty breathing/swallowing, symptoms >7–10 days, rash, drowsiness).

steps.title: Completing courses
steps.body: Take antibiotics exactly as prescribed; never share or keep leftovers.

a.text: Customer wants azithromycin without prescription for a cold. Response?

choices.label: Decline politely, explain viral cause and resistance, offer symptom care

b.text: He asks when he should worry.

choices.label: Safety-net: see a doctor for breathing or swallowing difficulty, high fever, or no improvement in 7–10 days

end1.text: He recovers in 5 days with symptomatic care.

Patients should do what with leftover antibiotics?
options: Not keep or share them; return for safe disposal

courses.title: Pharmacy Practice: Dispensing, Counselling & Calculations
courses.summary: Prescription screening, dispensing workflow, paediatric dose arithmetic, patient counselling and error prevention in community and hospital pharmacy.
outcomes: Learners can screen a prescription for legality and safety
Learners can calculate weight-based doses and liquid volumes
Learners can counsel patients using a structured method
Learners can report and prevent dispensing errors

scenes.text: A handwritten prescription has no patient age and an unclear drug name.
Screen before you dispense.

steps.title: Note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training or a professional licence.

steps.title: Screening checklist
steps.body: **Legal:** prescriber name, qualification, registration number, signature, date, patient name/age/sex/address. **Clinical:** right drug, dose, frequency, route, duration for this patient; allergies; interactions; duplications; pregnancy/breastfeeding; renal/hepatic function; children/elderly.

steps.title: Sound-alike look-alike (LASA)
steps.body: Pairs like hydroxyzine/hydralazine or similar brand names cause errors — confirm the indication with the patient or prescriber.

steps.title: When in doubt
steps.body: Contact the prescriber; never guess an unclear name or dose.

activity.prompt: Prescription screening steps
items: Check prescriber details, registration number and signature
Check date and patient details incl. age and weight for children
Confirm drug name, strength, dose, frequency, duration
Ask about allergies and current medicines
Clarify anything unclear with the prescriber

quiz.q: An unclear drug name should be…
For a child's prescription you especially need…
A legal prescription in India includes the prescriber's…

scenes.text: A prescription: 15 mg/kg per dose for a 12 kg child; suspension 120 mg/5 mL.
Calculate the volume to check the prescriber's order.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Dose = 15 × 12 = **180 mg**. Volume = 180 ÷ 120 × 5 = **7.5 mL**. Always check against the maximum single and daily dose on the label/formulary.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: 1) Weight-based dose (mg) = mg/kg × kg. 2) Volume = dose ÷ concentration (mg/mL). 3) Check units, decimal points and maximum doses. 4) Use an oral syringe for accuracy.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using the child's age instead of weight; confusing mg with mL; 10-fold decimal errors (0.5 vs 5 mL).

activity.prompt: Prescribed 10 mg/kg for a 16 kg child; suspension 200 mg/5 mL. Volume per dose (mL)?

quiz.q: Dose 250 mg; syrup 125 mg/5 mL → volume…
Best measuring device for children's liquids:

scenes.text: A teenager collects her first salbutamol MDI with a spacer.
Counsel her effectively.

steps.title: Structured counselling
steps.body: Introduce yourself; confirm identity; ask what the prescriber told her (prime questions); explain name and purpose, how and when to use, what to expect, common side effects (tremor, palpitations), what to do if not working, storage; demonstrate and use **teach-back**; offer written information.

steps.title: MDI with spacer technique
steps.body: Shake inhaler, remove cap, attach to spacer, breathe out gently, seal lips on mouthpiece, press once, breathe in slowly and deeply (or 4–5 tidal breaths), hold breath ~10 s if able; repeat per prescription after ~30–60 s.

steps.title: Red flags
steps.body: Reliever needed more often, waking at night, can't speak in sentences → seek urgent medical help; severe attack → 112.

activity.prompt: Order the MDI + spacer technique
items: Shake the inhaler and remove the cap
Breathe out gently away from the spacer
Breathe in slowly (or several tidal breaths)
Hold breath about 10 seconds if possible
Wait 30–60 seconds before a second puff if prescribed

quiz.q: Needing the reliever more often suggests…

options: Improving lung deposition and reducing throat deposition

scenes.text: A patient returns: her bottle says 5 mg but the prescription said 2.5 mg.
Handle the incident.

steps.title: Incident response
steps.body: Ensure patient safety first (has she taken any? any symptoms? contact prescriber/doctor), apologise and correct, document, report via the pharmacy's incident system, root cause analysis (look-alike stock, interruptions, no final check), implement fixes (separate shelving, barcode scanning, independent check).

steps.title: Pharmacovigilance
steps.body: Adverse drug reactions in India can be reported to the Pharmacovigilance Programme of India (PvPI).

steps.title: Just culture
steps.body: Focus on systems, not blame, while maintaining accountability.

ticket.description: My tablets say 5 mg but my doctor wrote 2.5. I took one this morning and feel a bit dizzy. Is it dangerous?
worknotes: Dispensed yesterday 18:40 during busy evening shift

investigate.label: Check the prescription and dispensing record
investigate.reveal: Rx: 2.5 mg once daily. Label and stock dispensed: 5 mg.

investigate.label: Check stock shelf layout
investigate.reveal: 2.5 mg and 5 mg packs of the same brand stored side by side, near-identical packaging.

investigate.label: Check the till receipt total
investigate.reveal: Price matches 5 mg pack; not relevant to safety.

investigate.label: Ask about symptoms and other medicines
investigate.reveal: Mild dizziness, no fainting; on no other BP medicines.

diagnosis.q: What is the main root cause?
options: Look-alike packaging stored together with no final strength check
diagnosis.why: System factors (adjacent LASA stock, busy shift, no independent check).

resolution: Assess patient safety and advise per prescriber/doctor (seek care if symptoms worsen)
Apologise and supply the correct 2.5 mg strength
Report through the incident reporting system
Separate LASA stock and add shelf alerts
Introduce a final strength check/barcode scan

closure.model: Root cause: 2.5 mg and 5 mg packs with similar packaging stored side by side; no final strength check during a busy shift. Patient outcome: one 5 mg dose taken, mild dizziness, prescriber informed, advised to monitor, correct strength supplied, follow-up call next day — symptoms resolved. Corrective action: stock separated with LASA alerts, barcode check before handover, shared at team meeting.

courses.title: Pharmacy Regulations & Ethics (General Overview)
courses.summary: A general-education overview of the laws and bodies that regulate medicines and pharmacy in India, prescription-only categories, controlled substances and professional ethics.
outcomes: Learners can name the main Indian laws governing drugs and pharmacy
Learners can describe prescription-only and controlled categories in general terms
Learners can explain record-keeping and storage duties
Learners can apply professional ethics to dilemmas

scenes.text: A new pharmacist wonders which law covers her licence and which covers the medicines she sells.
Several laws work together.

steps.title: Note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training or a professional licence.

steps.title: Key laws and bodies (general terms)
steps.body:
- **Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and Rules, 1945:** import, manufacture, distribution and sale of drugs; schedules such as H, H1 and X for prescription and record requirements; Schedule M for GMP. Central regulator: CDSCO (headed by the Drugs Controller General of India); state drug control departments license pharmacies.
- **Pharmacy Act, 1948:** registration of pharmacists; Pharmacy Council of India (PCI) regulates pharmacy education; state pharmacy councils maintain registers.
- **Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, 1985:** controls narcotic and psychotropic substances.
- **Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954:** restricts misleading advertisements.

steps.title: Rules change
steps.body: Regulations are updated by notifications; always check the current official text. This is general education, not legal advice.

steps.title: Pharmacovigilance
steps.body: PvPI collects ADR reports nationally.

activity.prompt: Match the law/body to its main role
pairs: Manufacture, distribution and sale of drugs
Control of narcotic and psychotropic substances

quiz.q: Registration of pharmacists is governed by the…

lessons.title: Lab: Prescription categories at the counter

scenes.text: Throughout the day customers ask for different medicines.
Apply the general categories.

steps.title: General categories
steps.body:
- **Schedule H:** prescription-only; sold only against a valid prescription.
- **Schedule H1:** a subset (e.g. certain antibiotics, anti-TB drugs, some habit-forming drugs) with additional requirements, including keeping a separate register with prescriber, patient and quantity details for a set period, and a warning label.
- **Schedule X:** stricter controls (certain psychotropic substances): prescription retention and special records.
- **Over-the-counter (non-scheduled):** may be sold without prescription, with counselling.

steps.title: Practice
steps.body: Even for OTC sales, ask WWHAM-style questions (Who, What symptoms, How long, Action taken, Medicines) and refer when needed.

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice; check the current schedules and state rules.

activity.prompt: General handling category
buckets: Can be advised OTC with counselling

items.text: Paracetamol tablets for a mild headache (label dose)

options: A police permit for every sale
A separate register with prescription details

lessons.title: Lab: Storage, cold chain and records

scenes.text: The pharmacy fridge shows 11 °C on Monday morning after a weekend power cut.
Vaccines and insulin are inside.

steps.title: Storage basics
steps.body: Store as labelled: room temperature (often below 25 °C or 30 °C as stated), refrigerated **2–8 °C** (vaccines, insulin, some biologics), protect from light/moisture. Monitor and record fridge min/max temperatures daily. Rotate stock (FEFO: first expiry, first out). Segregate expired/recalled stock.

steps.title: Cold chain excursion
steps.body: Quarantine affected items ('do not use'), record the excursion (temperature, duration), contact the manufacturer/supplier or programme officer for stability advice, and do not dispense until cleared.

steps.title: Never
steps.body: Never freeze vaccines unless specified; freezing destroys many (e.g. those with aluminium adjuvants).

activity.prompt: Order the response to a cold-chain excursion
items: Note current, min and max temperatures and time
Quarantine affected stock and label 'Do not use'
Dispose or release stock as advised

quiz.q: Refrigerated medicines are usually stored at…
After an excursion, affected vaccines should be…

scenes.text: A regular customer begs for sleeping tablets 'just this once' without a prescription.
Act ethically.

steps.title: Professional ethics
steps.body: Patient welfare first, honesty, confidentiality, competence, respect for autonomy, legality, no promotion of unnecessary medicines, refusal of inducements, and continuing professional development.

steps.title: Refusal with care
steps.body: Decline clearly, explain why, offer alternatives (sleep hygiene advice, referral to a doctor), and check for distress — share Tele-MANAS 14416 if appropriate.

steps.title: Confidentiality
steps.body: Never discuss a patient's medicines with others (including family) without consent, except where law or safety requires.

a.text: Customer requests a benzodiazepine without prescription. Response?

choices.label: Decline kindly, explain the law and risks, offer sleep advice and doctor referral
Give a few tablets since he's a regular

b.text: He says he hasn't slept for weeks since losing his job and feels hopeless.

choices.label: Listen, encourage seeing a doctor today, share Tele-MANAS 14416; if in danger, 112

end1.text: He calls Tele-MANAS and books a doctor's appointment.

uni-pharm-sciences.title: B.Pharm · Pharmaceutics, Pharmaceutical Chemistry & Pharmacognosy
uni-pharm-sciences.description: B.Pharm study companion for pharmaceutics, pharmaceutical calculations, pharmacokinetics, medicinal chemistry and analysis, and pharmacognosy — with verified numerical labs and QC decision labs. PCI subject names are topic tags only. A study companion only: it does not replace supervised clinical training or a licence.

courses.title: Pharmaceutics I: Dosage Forms & Pharmaceutical Calculations
courses.summary: Dosage form design, solutions, suspensions, emulsions, tablets and capsules, plus the calculations every pharmacist must get right: percentages, dilutions, alligation and isotonicity basics.
outcomes: Learners can classify dosage forms and their uses
Learners can solve percentage and ratio-strength problems
Learners can perform dilutions and alligation
Learners can identify formulation problems

scenes.text: An elderly patient cannot swallow tablets; a child needs a weight-based dose.
Dosage form choice solves both.

steps.title: Note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training or a professional licence.

steps.title: Classification
steps.body:
- **Solid:** tablets (compressed, film-coated, enteric-coated, sustained-release), capsules (hard, soft), powders, granules.
- **Liquid:** solutions (syrups, elixirs), suspensions (insoluble drug dispersed), emulsions (o/w, w/o).
- **Semisolid:** ointments, creams, gels, pastes, suppositories.
- **Sterile:** injections, eye drops, infusions.
- **Gaseous/aerosols:** inhalers.

steps.title: Key formulation ideas
steps.body: Suspensions need suspending agents and 'shake well' labels (sedimentation, caking; Stokes' law: settling rate ∝ particle radius² and density difference, inversely ∝ viscosity). Emulsions need emulsifiers; instability: creaming (reversible), cracking (irreversible), phase inversion. Enteric coats resist gastric acid.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Crushing a modified-release or enteric-coated tablet — this can cause dose dumping or gastric irritation. Check before crushing.

activity.prompt: Sort the dosage forms

quiz.q: By Stokes' law, sedimentation rate increases with…
Irreversible separation of an emulsion is…

scenes.text: A prescription asks for 100 mL of 0.5% w/v solution.
How many grams?

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- % **w/v** = g per 100 mL
- % **w/w** = g per 100 g
- % **v/v** = mL per 100 mL
- **Ratio strength** 1:1000 = 1 g in 1000 mL = 0.1% w/v.
- mg/mL = % w/v × 10.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Treating % w/v as mg per mL directly (2% is 20 mg/mL, not 2 mg/mL).

activity.prompt: How many grams of drug are needed to make 400 mL of a 2.5% w/v solution?

scenes.text: You need 500 mL of 70% v/v ethanol from 95% stock.
Use C1V1 = C2V2; then alligation for mixing two strengths.

steps.title: Dilution
steps.body: C1V1 = C2V2 → 95 × V1 = 70 × 500 → V1 = **368.4 mL** of 95% made up to 500 mL with water (volume contraction means 'make up to volume', not 'add 131.6 mL').

steps.title: Alligation medial (mixing two strengths)
steps.body: Mix 20% and 5% ointment to get 10%: parts of 20% = 10 − 5 = 5; parts of 5% = 20 − 10 = 10 → ratio **1:2**. For 300 g: 100 g of 20% + 200 g of 5%.

steps.title: Check

courses.title: Biopharmaceutics & Pharmacokinetics
courses.summary: ADME, bioavailability, one-compartment kinetics, half-life, volume of distribution, clearance and dosing-rate numericals.
outcomes: Learners can explain ADME processes
Learners can calculate half-life, Vd and clearance
Learners can compute bioavailability from AUC
Learners can reason about steady state and loading doses

scenes.text: Two brands of the same drug give different blood levels in a study.
Bioavailability explains why.

steps.title: Note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training or a professional licence.

steps.title: ADME
steps.body: **Absorption** (passive diffusion of unionised drug; pH partition), **distribution** (plasma protein binding, tissue binding, barriers), **metabolism** (phase I oxidation via CYP450, phase II conjugation; first-pass effect), **excretion** (renal: filtration, secretion, reabsorption; biliary).

steps.title: Bioavailability (F)
steps.body: Fraction of the dose reaching systemic circulation unchanged. Absolute F = (AUC_oral × Dose_IV) / (AUC_IV × Dose_oral). Bioequivalence compares AUC and Cmax of test vs reference (90% CI commonly within 80–125%).

activity.prompt: IV 50 mg gives AUC 20 mg·h/L; oral 100 mg gives AUC 30 mg·h/L. Absolute bioavailability (%)?

quiz.q: First-pass metabolism mainly reduces bioavailability of…
Bioequivalence usually requires 90% CI of AUC and Cmax ratios within…

scenes.text: A drug's elimination rate constant is 0.1 h⁻¹.
Find the half-life.

steps.title: First-order kinetics
steps.body: C = C0·e^(−kt); **t½ = 0.693 / k**. After 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 half-lives about 50, 75, 87.5, 93.75, 96.9% is eliminated — steady state is reached in about 4–5 half-lives with repeated dosing.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
k = 0.1 h⁻¹ → t½ = **6.93 h**.
C0 = 80 mg/L, t½ = 4 h → after 12 h (3 half-lives) C = 80/8 = **10 mg/L**.

steps.title: Zero-order
steps.body: Some drugs (ethanol, high-dose phenytoin, high-dose aspirin) show saturable, zero-order elimination: a constant amount per hour, half-life not constant.

activity.prompt: Initial plasma concentration 64 mg/L, half-life 3 h. Concentration after 9 h?

quiz.q: t½ when k = 0.2 h⁻¹ is about…
Steady state is reached after about…
A drug with zero-order elimination at high doses is…

lessons.title: Lab: Volume of distribution and clearance

scenes.text: A 500 mg IV bolus gives an initial concentration of 10 mg/L.
Calculate Vd, then clearance.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body: **Vd = Dose / C0**. **CL = k × Vd** = 0.693 × Vd / t½. **Loading dose = Vd × target C** (÷ F if oral). **Maintenance dose rate = CL × target Css** (÷ F).

steps.title: Interpretation
steps.body: Large Vd (≫ total body water ~42 L in 70 kg adult) → extensive tissue binding; small Vd → drug stays in plasma (high protein binding).

activity.prompt: A 300 mg IV bolus gives C0 = 6 mg/L. What is the volume of distribution?

quiz.q: Clearance with k = 0.1 h⁻¹ and Vd = 40 L:
Maintenance dose rate depends mainly on…

scenes.text: A drug: Vd 35 L, t½ 7 h, oral F 0.7, target Css 10 mg/L.
Work through all parameters.

steps.title: Step-by-step
steps.body:
k = 0.693/7 = 0.099 h⁻¹; CL = 0.099 × 35 = 3.47 L/h.
Oral loading dose = Vd × C / F = 35 × 10 / 0.7 = **500 mg**.
Oral maintenance rate = CL × Css / F = 3.47 × 10 / 0.7 ≈ **49.5 mg/h** ≈ 1188 mg/day (illustrative; real dosing follows the product label and clinician).

steps.title: Renal impairment
steps.body: If clearance halves, maintenance rate halves for the same target; Vd and loading dose often unchanged.

steps.title: Reminder
steps.body: These are textbook numericals, not dosing instructions for patients.

courses.title: Pharmaceutical Chemistry: Drug Classes, SAR & Analysis
courses.summary: Medicinal chemistry essentials (functional groups, SAR of key classes), impurity limits, titrimetric and instrumental analysis used in quality control.
outcomes: Learners can link structure to activity for key drug classes
Learners can perform titration-based assay calculations
Learners can choose analytical techniques for QC
Learners can interpret a certificate of analysis

scenes.text: A penicillin stops working against a bacterium that makes β-lactamase.
The β-lactam ring is both the weapon and the weak spot.

steps.title: Note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training or a professional licence.

steps.title: β-lactams
steps.body: The four-membered **β-lactam ring** acylates penicillin-binding proteins (transpeptidases) blocking cell-wall cross-linking. β-lactamases hydrolyse the ring; inhibitors such as clavulanic acid protect it. Bulky side chains (e.g. in methicillin-type drugs) resist some β-lactamases.

steps.title: Other SAR highlights
steps.body:
- **Sulfonamides:** para-amino group essential (mimic PABA).
- **Catecholamines:** catechol OH groups for receptor binding; N-substitution size shifts α → β selectivity (larger groups → more β).
- **Benzodiazepines:** electron-withdrawing group at position 7 increases activity.
- **Fluoroquinolones:** fluorine at C-6 broadens spectrum and potency.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Thinking clavulanic acid is itself a strong antibiotic — it is mainly a β-lactamase inhibitor.

activity.prompt: Match the structural feature to the drug class

scenes.text: QC assays aspirin tablets by acid–base titration.
Calculate % label claim.

steps.title: Assay calculation
steps.body: Amount of drug = titre (mL) × molarity factor × equivalence factor (mg per mL of titrant). % label claim = (found ÷ labelled) × 100. Pharmacopoeial limits are typically like 95–105% for many tablets (check the monograph).

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Each mL of 0.1 M NaOH ≡ 18.02 mg aspirin (1:1, MW 180.16). Titre 16.5 mL with exactly 0.1 M → 16.5 × 18.02 = **297.3 mg** per tablet; label 300 mg → **99.1%**.

steps.title: Correction factor
steps.body: If titrant is 0.1020 M instead of 0.1000 M, multiply by 1.02.

activity.prompt: Each mL of 0.1 M titrant ≡ 15.0 mg drug. Titre 32.0 mL of exactly 0.1 M. Label claim 500 mg. % label claim?

quiz.q: Titrant 0.105 M instead of 0.100 M: correction factor…
Limits for assay are found in the…

scenes.text: Five QC questions arrive on the same day.
Pick the right instrument for each.

steps.title: Techniques
steps.body:
- **UV–Visible spectrophotometry:** assay via Beer–Lambert (A = εbc).
- **HPLC:** assay and related-substance impurities, content uniformity.
- **IR:** identification (fingerprint region).
- **Karl Fischer titration:** water content.
- **GC:** residual solvents.
- **Dissolution apparatus:** release testing.
- **AAS/ICP:** elemental impurities.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Using UV alone to quantify an impurity that co-absorbs with the drug — separation (HPLC) is needed.

scenes.text: A CoA for an API batch lands on your desk.
Decide if it meets specification.

steps.title: CoA elements
steps.body: Product, batch number, manufacture and retest/expiry dates, tests with specifications and results: description, identification, assay, related substances, water, residual solvents, heavy/elemental metals, microbial limits, sign-off by QA.

steps.title: Decision rule
steps.body: Any out-of-specification (OOS) result → investigation per SOP; never 're-test into compliance' without justification.

steps.title: GMP
steps.body: Schedule M (India) and WHO GMP require documented investigations and QA release.

courses.title: Pharmacognosy & Phytochemistry
courses.summary: Crude drugs, classes of plant constituents, identification tests, standardisation and safety of herbal medicines.
outcomes: Learners can classify crude drugs and their constituents
Learners can match drugs to their active principles
Learners can apply chemical identification tests
Learners can evaluate herbal products for quality and safety

scenes.text: Digitalis leaves, cinchona bark and senna pods all gave modern medicines.
Their power lies in specific constituents.

steps.title: Note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training or a professional licence.

steps.title: Major constituent classes
steps.body:
- **Alkaloids** (basic N): morphine (opium), quinine (cinchona), atropine (belladonna), reserpine (Rauwolfia), vincristine (Catharanthus).
- **Glycosides:** cardiac (digoxin from Digitalis), anthraquinone (sennosides from senna), cyanogenic.
- **Tannins**, **volatile oils** (clove: eugenol; peppermint: menthol), **resins**, **flavonoids**, **terpenoids** (artemisinin from Artemisia annua).

steps.title: Classification approaches
steps.body: Alphabetical, morphological (leaves, barks, roots), taxonomical, pharmacological, chemical.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Calling sennosides alkaloids — they are anthraquinone glycosides.

activity.prompt: Match the crude drug to its key constituent

scenes.text: A student extract is suspected to contain alkaloids.
Run chemical tests.

steps.title: General tests
steps.body:
- Alkaloids: **Dragendorff's** (orange-red precipitate), **Mayer's** (cream precipitate), **Wagner's** (reddish-brown), Hager's (yellow).
- Anthraquinones: **Borntrager's test** (pink/red in ammonia layer).
- Cardiac glycosides: **Keller–Killiani** (reddish-brown ring at interface, blue-green upper layer — deoxy sugars).
- Tannins: ferric chloride (blue-black/green).
- Steroids/triterpenoids: Liebermann–Burchard, Salkowski.
- Starch: iodine (blue-black).

steps.title: Interpretation
steps.body: Tests can give false positives (e.g. proteins with alkaloid reagents); confirm with TLC/HPLC.

steps.title: Safety
steps.body: Handle reagents (e.g. concentrated acids) with PPE in a fume hood.

activity.prompt: Match the test to what it detects

quiz.q: Mayer's reagent gives a … precipitate with alkaloids
Chemical test positives should be confirmed by…

scenes.text: A cheap 'ashwagandha root powder' looks suspicious.
Run standardisation checks.

steps.title: Evaluation methods
steps.body: Organoleptic (colour, odour, taste), microscopic (characteristic cells, stomata, trichomes, starch grains), physical (ash values — total, acid-insoluble; extractive values; moisture/loss on drying; foreign matter), chemical (marker compounds, TLC/HPTLC fingerprint), biological, and contaminants (heavy metals, pesticides, aflatoxins, microbial load).

steps.title: Ash values
steps.body: High acid-insoluble ash suggests sand/soil contamination.

steps.title: Adulteration
steps.body: Substitution with cheaper species, exhausted drugs, or synthetic drug spiking (e.g. steroids in 'herbal' remedies) are real risks.

story.title: St John's wort and the pill

scenes.text: A customer taking an oral contraceptive asks about starting St John's wort.
Counsel safely.

steps.title: Key interactions
steps.body:
- **St John's wort:** induces CYP3A4 and P-gp → reduced levels of oral contraceptives, ciclosporin, warfarin, some antiretrovirals; serotonin syndrome risk with SSRIs.
- **Ginkgo, garlic** (high doses): may increase bleeding risk with anticoagulants/antiplatelets.
- **Grapefruit juice** (food): inhibits intestinal CYP3A4 → raised levels of some statins, calcium-channel blockers.

steps.title: Counselling
steps.body: Ask about all herbal and OTC products; 'natural' does not mean safe. Refer to the prescriber when an interaction is significant.

steps.title: Documentation
steps.body: Record herbal use in the medication history.

x.text: Reconsider: enzyme induction lowers hormone levels.
